passages.t: A flask of oil at Ramoth-gilead
passages.happening:
Elisha sends one of the sons of the prophets to Ramoth-gilead with a flask of oil. He is to find Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, take him into an inner room, pour the oil on his head and say that the LORD anoints him king over Israel, then open the door and run (verses 1-3).

The young prophet finds the army commanders sitting together and takes Jehu inside. He pours the oil and speaks the LORD's word: Jehu is to strike down the house of Ahab, ‘so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by the hand of Jezebel’ (verse 7). The whole house of Ahab will perish, and dogs will devour Jezebel at Jezreel, with no one to bury her (verses 8-10). Then he runs.

The officers ask Jehu, “Is everything all right? Why did this madman come to you?” (verse 11). Jehu tries to brush it off, then tells them. At once each man spreads his garment under Jehu on the bare steps, they blow the ram's horn, and they proclaim, “Jehu is king!” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The long story of Ahab's house, begun in 1 Kings 16, reaches its end. At Horeb Elijah had been told to anoint Jehu king of Israel. After Naboth's murder Elijah announced that dogs would eat Jezebel at Jezreel and that every male of Ahab's line would be cut off. God delayed that judgment when Ahab humbled himself. Now, in the days of Ahab's son, it falls.

Jehu's coup came in 841 BC, one of the firmest dates of the period. That same year Shalmaneser III of Assyria received tribute from Jehu. The Black Obelisk, found at Nimrud in 1846, shows a figure bowing before the Assyrian king with a caption naming Jehu, son of Omri; the Assyrians went on calling Israel the house of Omri after his dynasty had fallen.

Anointing with oil set a person apart for an office, especially kingship. The verb, mashach, lies behind mashiach, anointed one, from which the word Messiah comes. Here it marks God's choice and commission for one task of judgment, not the character of the man anointed. Done in secret in an inner room, it made Jehu king in God's sight before anyone cheered. The officers call the prophet a madman, which shows how prophets could look to outsiders. Garments laid down on the steps made a makeshift royal carpet, and the ram's horn announced a new king.
passages.later: Samuel had anointed David ‘in the presence of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward’ (1 Samuel 16:13). No such words are said of Jehu.
passages.asks: Jehu was anointed for a task, and the anointing did not make him a good man. Ask whether you mistake being useful to God for being right with God. And ask what task you have been given that could go wrong if your heart is not in it.

passages.t: Driving like a madman to Jezreel
passages.happening:
King Joram is at Jezreel recovering from wounds he took fighting Hazael, and Ahaziah king of Judah has gone down to visit him (verses 14-16). Jehu sets out in his chariot. The watchman on the tower sees his troops coming. Joram sends a horseman to ask, ‘Have you come in peace?’ (verse 17). Jehu answers, “What do you know about peace?” (verse 18), and tells the rider to fall in behind him. A second horseman does the same. Then the watchman says, “he is driving like a madman!” (verse 20), and knows it is Jehu.

Joram and Ahaziah ride out, each in his own chariot, and meet Jehu ‘on the property of Naboth the Jezreelite’ (verse 21). Joram asks, “Have you come in peace, Jehu?” Jehu answers, “How can there be peace,” ‘as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel abound?’ (verse 22). Joram turns to flee, crying treachery to Ahaziah (verse 23), and Jehu shoots him dead in his chariot (verse 24). He has the body thrown into Naboth's field, ‘according to the word of the LORD’ (verse 26).

Ahaziah flees. Jehu's men shoot him near Ibleam, and he reaches Megiddo and dies there. His servants carry him to Jerusalem and bury him in the City of David (verses 27-28).
passages.hearers:
Ramoth-gilead lay east of the Jordan, so the ride to Jezreel, a royal residence in the fertile valley, covered a long distance. Ibleam and Megiddo lay along the valley's edge. Ahaziah of Judah was Ahab's grandson through his mother Athaliah, and he dies because he was visiting his wounded uncle. The chapter shows the fruit of Judah's alliance with Ahab's house.

The chapter is told at speed, and peace, shalom, is its refrain. Joram's riders ask it, Joram asks it, and later Jezebel asks it. Jehu turns the greeting into a verdict: there is no peace where the covenant is broken by idolatry and violence.

Place is loaded. Joram meets Jehu on Naboth's land, and his body is thrown onto Naboth's plot. The word for the plot, cheleq, ties the judgment to the ground Ahab took. Jehu quotes the LORD's word as he does it. He is shown as energetic, ruthless and quick with Scripture, a portrait that is not simply admiring.

Second Chronicles 22:7-9 tells Ahaziah's death somewhat differently, with him found hiding in Samaria and brought to Jehu. Interpreters have proposed ways to fit the two together, and some see them as separate traditions.
passages.later: After Naboth's murder Elijah had told Ahab, ‘Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?’ (1 Kings 21:19). God told Cain, ‘The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground’ (Genesis 4:10).
passages.hard:
The Tel Dan Stele seems to credit an Aramean king with killing Joram and Ahaziah. Does that contradict this chapter? And how should a reader take Jehu's bloodshed?

The Tel Dan Stele is an Aramaic inscription found in fragments at Tel Dan in northern Israel in 1993 and 1994. In it a king of Aram, most likely Hazael, boasts that he killed a king of Israel and a king of the house of David. Most scholars restore the damaged names as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Jehoram, which seems to conflict with this chapter, where Jehu kills both. Several explanations have been offered. Jehu may have acted in some kind of alliance with Hazael, or at least in the setting of Hazael's war, so that Hazael could claim the deaths as his own victory; Joram's wounds came from the Arameans. Ancient royal inscriptions often claimed credit for events their kings did not carry out in person. Or the two accounts may keep different traditions that cannot be fully fitted together. Both agree that Joram and Ahaziah died violently in the same upheaval, about 841 BC. The stele also holds the earliest known mention outside the Bible of the house of David.

As for Jehu, the chapter presents his coup as the fulfillment of the LORD's word against Ahab's house for innocent blood, and it also shows him killing a king of Judah who was not named in that word. About a century later Hosea named his son Jezreel, ‘for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu’ (Hosea 1:4). Chapter 10 takes up how the two verdicts fit. Being used by God to bring judgment does not make anyone righteous, and nothing here gives anyone a warrant to kill a ruler, an opponent or anyone else in God's name.
passages.asks: Jehu told Joram there could be no peace while the wrong at the root went on. Ask what false peace you keep while ignoring what is wrong underneath. And ask whether you are quick with Scripture in a way that serves your own plans.

passages.happening:
Jehu comes to Jezreel. Jezebel hears of it, paints her eyes, arranges her hair, and looks down from a window (verse 30). As he enters the gate she asks, “Have you come in peace, O Zimri, murderer of your master?” (verse 31). Jehu looks up and calls, “Who is on my side? Who?” (verse 32). Two or three of her own servants look down, and at his order they throw her from the window. She dies in the street (verse 33).

Jehu goes in to eat and drink. Then he says to bury her, ‘for she was the daughter of a king’ (verse 34). But when they go out, almost nothing of her is left (verse 35). Jehu says it is the word of the LORD spoken through Elijah, that the dogs would devour Jezebel at Jezreel (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Jezebel's painted eyes and arranged hair have been read as an attempt to seduce or manipulate Jehu, or, more likely in context, as a queen dressing in royal dignity to face death. Calling him Zimri was a curse and a warning. Zimri was the commander who killed King Elah and reigned only seven days.

To lie unburied and be eaten by dogs was among the worst fates in the ancient world, a sign of total rejection. Jehu's order to bury her came too late. The chapter is framed by prophecy: it begins with the young prophet's word that dogs would eat Jezebel at Jezreel, and it ends with Jehu quoting Elijah's word as fulfilled. Her worship of Baal had not been only private belief. It came with the corruption of justice that killed Naboth.
passages.later: In Revelation the risen Christ uses her name for a false prophetess at Thyatira: ‘You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess’ (Revelation 2:20).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take Jezebel's death?

The text tells it in a few verses and does not linger, and these notes do the same. It presents her death as the word Elijah spoke after Naboth's murder coming true: she had used the forms of law to kill an innocent man and had led a royal campaign against the LORD's prophets. The chapter does not ask the reader to enjoy it. Jehu eats and drinks before he thinks of burial, and the narrator lets that detail stand.

Nothing here gives anyone a warrant to harm a woman, a ruler or anyone else, or to treat a person's death as a spectacle. Her name in Revelation is a warning about false teaching, not a label to throw at any woman today.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jezebel's question about peace came too late, after a lifetime of violence. Ask what it would mean to seek peace with God now rather than at the end. And ask whether you treat the fall of people you dislike as something to enjoy.
